hero.headline: Florida Supreme Court adopts new AI courtroom rules after fabricated evidence cases
hero.teaser: Florida attorneys and self-represented litigants will be required to certify that what they cite in court exists and is accurate starting June 15.
hero.body:
The Florida Supreme Court has adopted new rules to address the misuse of artificial intelligence in legal proceedings, marking a response to what legal experts describe as a growing crisis. The regulations take effect June 15 and require attorneys and self-represented litigants to certify that any citations and evidence they present in court are accurate and exist. Violations could result in sanctions ranging from public reprimands to fines and suspension from practice.

Federal Judge William Matthewman, chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, has worked to combat AI misuse in courts after witnessing its widespread problems firsthand. "It's really a problem," Matthewman said, expressing concern about the trajectory of the issue. "Unfortunately, I see it getting worse before it gets better. I think the Florida Supreme Court's order will help in Florida, but I unfortunately have seen over the last couple of years that it is growing and growing and growing." He urged lawyers and self-represented parties to verify everything before filing, warning they could face serious consequences otherwise.

The rules emerged after several high-profile incidents highlighted the dangers of unverified AI-generated content in courtrooms. In Polk County, an attorney representing the school district in a lawsuit over school bus cameras was criticized after a judge found fabricated facts and nonexistent case citations in a motion to dismiss. The attorney acknowledged using ChatGPT as a drafting and research tool but stated there was no excuse for failing to verify the information before submission. The school district indicated it would review whether the attorney would remain eligible for future contracts. Additionally, a St. Petersburg woman was arrested after using AI to create a false photo of a man she accused of burglary and rape, later admitting the image was fabricated.

Criminal defense attorney Paul Figueroa in Tampa, who recently began using AI to enhance his workflow, acknowledges the technology's limitations. "It can be something as simple as it gives a quote that's directly on point to my case, and you go, all right, this is brilliant, this is what I've been looking for, I could have searched 300 cases and not come up with anything better than this, and then you realize that's not in the case," Figueroa explained. When asked if the new rules sufficiently address the problem, Figueroa believes they do for the current situation. Judge Matthewman's warning remains clear: anyone filing court documents must ensure accuracy or risk serious legal consequences.

cards.headline: Florida considers statewide fireworks ban for Fourth of July's 250th anniversary due to severe drought
cards.body:
Florida state leaders are examining whether to implement a statewide ban on fireworks for this year's Fourth of July celebration as drought conditions have reached levels not seen since 1998, when the state last prohibited fireworks across the entire state. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services has determined that current drought conditions are even more severe than those that prompted the 1998 ban. Every part of Florida is experiencing at least abnormally dry conditions, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast facing moderate to extreme drought situations.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson warned about the potential ban earlier in the year, recognizing both the importance of celebrating the nation's 250th anniversary and the serious fire risks posed by widespread fireworks use. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said in May. He emphasized that officials should explore alternative celebration methods, saying "We all love the 250th celebration we're gonna have this year, but we probably ought to be considering alternatives."

Despite the drought concerns, Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach has experienced increased customer activity as people prepare for the holiday. Bill Murphy, who works at the store, said the business closely monitors drought conditions to determine whether it is safe for fireworks use. Murphy expressed cautious optimism about the situation, pointing to weather forecasts that predict significant rainfall. "We always keep a close eye on the drought index to make sure the ground is saturated enough, but the reality is there's plenty of rain in the forecast," Murphy said.

The Department of Agriculture has indicated that a statewide fireworks ban would be a last resort measure, though the severity of current drought conditions has prompted serious deliberation about whether such action will become necessary. State officials continue to monitor conditions as the Fourth of July approaches to determine whether celebrating the nation's 250th anniversary will require residents to find alternatives to traditional fireworks displays.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban begins Monday in Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties
cards.teaser: A ban on fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen takes effect across the Treasure Coast on June 30 to reduce nutrient runoff during the rainy season.
cards.body:
Starting Monday, residents in Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties will be prohibited from using any fertilizer that contains phosphorus or nitrogen. The restriction applies to both residential lawns and landscaping projects throughout the three-county area.

According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the ban aims to decrease nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season. Excessive nutrients in stormwater runoff can trigger algae blooms in local waterways. The Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River are particularly vulnerable to these blooms, which can damage the ecological health of these important water systems. Algae blooms block sunlight from reaching beneficial aquatic plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. In more severe cases, harmful algae blooms produce toxins that pose risks to human health, wildlife, and the overall ecosystem.

Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a practical alternative during the ban period. Rather than relying on chemical fertilizers, residents can use compost to naturally enhance their gardens and landscaping. Ricketts suggests that a small trash can is an accessible and effective method for composting kitchen and yard waste, making it easy for homeowners to add nutrients to their landscape without breaking the law.

The fertilizer ban represents a concerted effort by the three counties to protect local waterways from nutrient pollution during the months when heavy rainfall increases the risk of runoff entering rivers, lagoons, and coastal areas. Residents who use their outdoor spaces for gardening and landscaping should prepare now by transitioning to composting methods before the ban takes effect.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowner's security camera catches masked burglar in real-time, leads to arrest
cards.teaser: A Port St.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested Thursday afternoon after a homeowner's security camera caught him burglarizing an apartment in real-time. Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling following the incident at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in the 5400 block of NW Moorehen Trail. The incident began around 3:38 p.m. when the apartment resident received a motion alert from his security system while away from home. Upon checking his live camera feed, the resident spotted a masked man inside his apartment. The resident activated his camera's audible siren, causing the suspect to leave briefly, only to return and tamper with the camera itself.

Multiple witnesses saw the suspect flee the victim's apartment and enter a neighboring unit in the same building. When Port St. Lucie Police arrived, they found clear signs of forced entry, including damage to the front door and door frame. Officers quickly established a perimeter while the SWAT team was called to assist. After repeated announcements, Thibodeau exited the apartment and surrendered without incident. Investigators collected surveillance footage from multiple sources throughout the complex, including doorbell cameras that captured a man matching the suspect's description before and after the burglary. Police found evidence that Thibodeau had attempted to obstruct security cameras and that a watch valued at approximately $300 was stolen during the burglary. Thibodeau was transported to the St. Lucie County Jail.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island Faces Critical Erosion Threatening to Split Island at Peck Lake
cards.teaser: A new state report warns nearly the entire 11.5-mile coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with the ocean potentially breaking through at Peck Lake and splitting the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater.

Among sites at risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site the report says is already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St. Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry said there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in those areas. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project. Field said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year, and the recent FDEP assessment positions Jupiter Island to better compete for state and federal funding to mitigate erosion.

cards.headline: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings suspends gubernatorial campaign after prostate cancer diagnosis
cards.teaser: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings announced he has been diagnosed with prostate cancer and is suspending his gubernatorial campaign, drawing messages of support from Republicans and Democrats across Florida.
cards.body:
Political allies and rivals across party lines are expressing support for Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings following his prostate cancer diagnosis and decision to suspend his gubernatorial campaign. Republican gubernatorial front-runner Byron Donalds wrote on X that he hopes "the Lord watch over the Demings family, provide them with strength and comfort, and bless Jerry with a swift recovery." Former U.S. Representative David Jolly, who faced Demings in the Democratic primary, said Demings has dedicated his life to public service and will bring that same spirit to this new chapter.

U.S. Rep. Maxwell Frost, an Orlando Democrat, wrote that Demings has always been a fighter for Orange County and will face this challenge with the same strength. Democrat state Sen. Shevrin Jones said Demings has spent a lifetime showing up for others and now it's their turn to support him. Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava called Demings a man of extraordinary strength demonstrated throughout his decades in law enforcement and public office. Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback said he and his wife will keep Demings in their prayers throughout treatment. Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said Demings has served with commitment and compassion for decades. Florida GOP Chair Evan Power also asked for prayers for Demings and his family. Governor Ron DeSantis, whose administration once threatened to remove Demings to pressure him into signing an immigration agreement, did not immediately post a statement on social media about the diagnosis.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion threatens to split island in half at Peck Lake, state report warns
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report reveals that nearly Jupiter Island's entire coastline faces critical erosion, endangering infrastructure, ecosystems, wildlife and archaeological sites. The assessment found the island's 11.5-mile shoreline has deteriorated so severely that ocean water could break through at Peck Lake, potentially dividing the barrier island in two. The threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breakthrough would transform a narrow land strip into an open inlet. This scenario has historical precedent. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers restored it with sand fill. Mark Perry from the Florida Oceanographic Society warns that another breach would destabilize ecosystems requiring a precise balance between fresh and saltwater to function. He also notes the consequences reach far beyond the shoreline itself.

The stakes include significant natural and cultural resources. The Joseph Reed Mound, an archaeological site dating back 3,000 to 4,000 years, has already lost half its mass to erosion. Wildlife refuges at risk include Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry points out that over 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. A separate state assessment indicates erosion threatens mangrove swamps essential for habitat and coastal defense, while elevated water levels could displace entire species across the island. Perry emphasizes that sea levels have risen since the 1950s and have accelerated over the last 15 years, requiring collaborative approaches to address the problem.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field confirmed the town battles erosion through continuous maintenance efforts. In April 2025, the community completed a substantial beach renourishment initiative, adding sand equivalent to filling nearly 400 Olympic-sized pools. While oceanfront homes face no immediate danger, Field stressed this security depends entirely on ongoing maintenance work. He characterized the current approach as repeatedly applying a temporary solution. About $3 million in local taxpayer funding supports beach renourishment annually. Field cautioned that a potential breach would demand significant state and federal investment for repairs. He indicated the recent FDEP assessment strengthens Jupiter Island's position to secure state and federal funding for erosion mitigation efforts.

Field emphasized that sustained funding remains uncertain. He warned that discontinuing beach renourishment support would trigger rapid and widespread coastal changes across Florida that residents would likely regret. The island's future depends on maintaining this investment in protective measures.

cards.headline: Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties face hundreds of millions in losses under property tax ballot measure
cards.teaser: Treasure Coast counties are working to calculate the financial impact of a November ballot measure that would raise the homestead exemption and sharply reduce p.
cards.body:
Government officials across the Treasure Coast are assessing the impact of a November property tax referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and reduce property tax revenue. According to a study from the Florida Association of Counties, Martin County would lose $50 million in the 2027-28 fiscal year and $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County would lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County would lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said officials are working with the Office of Management and Budget to determine the full financial impact. "If there's a cut when it comes to property taxes, there's going to be some real shortfalls, some real challenges and some revenue is going to have to be made up somewhere," Powell said.

The referendum proposes raising the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Powell noted that potential solutions to offset losses could include finding new revenue, increasing sales tax, or raising user fees for services. Florida law restricts local officials from speaking against or endorsing the referendum, though they can provide educational information. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the measure provides relief for struggling families. The homestead exemption savings for homeowners can vary from hundreds to thousands of dollars depending on the county, city, and assessed home value. In Palm Beach County, over half of properties have the homestead exemption, compared to the state average of 47%.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island officials say town prepared despite report warning of 9 feet of flooding at emergency center
cards.teaser: Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town is prepared for storms despite a state report warning that the Emergency Operations Center could see up to 9 feet of floodwater.
cards.body:
A new vulnerability assessment by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection identified 103 critical town assets at risk of flooding on Jupiter Island, including 68 stormwater facilities, 17 historic sites, conservation lands, and key evacuation routes. The 126-page report warned that the town's Emergency Operations Center could see up to 9 feet of floodwater. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the findings confirm what town leaders already knew, which is why they requested the assessment. Beach District Director John Duchok said the vulnerability assessment will set up a roadmap for how to adapt and tackle the highest priorities first.

Field said the goal is to document the risks, build a roadmap for improvements, and compete for state and federal funding to fix vulnerabilities. A funding application window opened June 1, and the town intends to apply. He said evacuation orders would be issued well before floodwaters threaten roadways, and the town has a backup facility on the mainland to maintain operations during emergencies. The report warned that stormwater systems face some of the greatest risks, noting they can fail during the very flooding events they are designed to manage. Field said improving drainage infrastructure along North Beach Road and potentially transitioning from septic to sewer systems are among the town's top priorities moving forward.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition begins as neighbors watch mixed-use redevelopment take shape
cards.teaser: Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project featuring retail, restaurants, and possible residential spaces.
cards.body:
Crews this week began demolishing portions of the Indian River Mall to make way for a revitalization project. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager for the redevelopment, said the first phase involves taking down the Macy's and soon, where the Sears used to be. Neighbors Mary Alice Stopyra and Mark Manera from Vero Beach watched the demolition in the mall's parking lot. Stopyra said she was happy about the teardown because the mall "has degraded over time." Manera, who has visited the mall for years, described it as looking "like the death of a beautiful building" and "more like a graveyard," noting a steady decline year after year.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with approximately 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants, and possible residential spaces. "They're not going to see a dead mall for the last 12 years that was getting cobwebs," Scarfone said, calling it "a city within a city." He hopes to complete the first phase by 2027, though crews are still working on permitting for the rest of the project. Manera said if the new development brings "new life, new jobs, new opportunity, that's wonderful."

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup, Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard claims she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee and developed parasitic infections.
cards.body:
An Okeechobee County woman is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after claiming she and her daughter found live worms in a can of SpaghettiOs purchased in June 2024. Mary Hubbard bought the product at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to the lawsuit, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food and documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the product.

Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications after eating the SpaghettiOs. The lawsuit seeks $50,000 in damages and alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell Soup said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development is already at risk, to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater to survive, and that conservation lands and historical and prehistorical sites are at risk.

According to the report, the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site, is already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges like Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry said there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in all of those areas. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field said no oceanfront homes are in immediate danger only because of that ongoing work. About $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year.

cards.headline: Fourth of July fireworks could be banned statewide due to drought conditions
cards.teaser: State leaders are watching drought conditions closely as they weigh whether to ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence, with the entire state of Florida at least abnormally dry.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look significantly different this year as state leaders monitor drought conditions to determine whether to ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services reports that this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was implemented. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about a potential ban in May, stating that if drought conditions persist through Fourth of July, a ban is likely. Simpson cautioned that hundreds of thousands of people using fireworks simultaneously could ignite fires across the entire state in a single evening. While acknowledging the significance of this year's 250th celebration, Simpson urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, owner Bill Murphy reported increased early shopping activity. Murphy said the store monitors the drought index closely to ensure adequate ground saturation but noted that substantial rain is forecasted. The Department of Agriculture characterized a fireworks ban as a last resort.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications after finding live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee.
cards.body:
An Okeechobee County woman is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after she and her daughter allegedly found live worms in SpaghettiOs they purchased in June 2024. Mary Hubbard bought the product at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to the complaint, she discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food. Hubbard documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product.

Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications from the incident. The lawsuit seeks $50,000 in damages and alleges that Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance program overwhelmed by demand as costs rise
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives nearly 8,000 calls per month for housing assistance, but the demand far outweighs the resources available.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program, designed to help residents who can't pay rent. Program director Dr. James Green told WPTV that demand far outweighs available resources. The county receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month based on data combined with 211. Currently, about 800 applications are in the queue for rental assistance, with approximately 600 applications typically received in the first couple of hours after applications open at the beginning of each month. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked CLOSED due to high demand. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Green said the recent surge in applications is partly due to rising costs of living, including housing, gas, and food. For those unable to access the county program, 211 is another option available 24/7 that connects callers with nonprofits and other assistance programs in the area. Green emphasized that preventing homelessness depends on everyone and called on people with extra housing to partner with the county to help neighbors in need.

hero.headline: Martin and St. Lucie Counties Fertilizer Ban Takes Effect June 1 Through September 30
hero.teaser: Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have banned fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen from June 1 through September 30 to reduce nutrient runoff during rainy season.
hero.body:
Starting June 1 and continuing through September 30, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. The seasonal restriction applies to both lawn care and landscaping projects throughout the ban period.

The ban exists to address a significant environmental concern during Florida's rainy season. Jordan Skaggs, who works with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that the restriction helps reduce nutrient-rich runoff that flows into local waterways. When these excess nutrients enter bodies of water, they can trigger harmful algae blooms that damage the ecosystem. The Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River are particularly vulnerable to these blooms, which can disrupt the natural balance these waterways depend on.

According to Skaggs, the consequences of harmful algae blooms extend far beyond visual pollution. These blooms can block out sunlight that beneficial plants need to survive, threatening the food sources that fish and wildlife depend on. In severe cases where blooms reach certain densities, they can produce toxins that pose risks to human health, harm wildlife populations, and damage the overall ecosystem. By reducing the nutrients that feed these blooms, the seasonal ban helps protect these important waterways and the communities that depend on them.

Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective alternative during the ban months. Ricketts noted that composting can provide the nutrients that landscapes and gardens need without relying on commercial fertilizers. He described a small trash can as the most practical approach, saying "It is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." This composting method allows residents to maintain their gardens and landscaping while complying with the county restrictions and protecting local water quality.

cards.headline: Indian River County Recycling Club Announces 2026 College Scholarship Opportunities
cards.teaser: The Recycling Club of Indian River County has announced college scholarship opportunities for 2026.
cards.body:
The Recycling Club of Indian River County has announced college scholarship opportunities for 2026. The scholarships are available to students in Indian River County.

The Recycling Club of Indian River County focuses on environmental education and recycling initiatives in the community. The scholarship program supports students pursuing higher education.

The announcement was made Friday. Students interested in applying can seek information from the Recycling Club of Indian River County.

The scholarship program represents the organization's commitment to supporting local students while promoting environmental awareness. Indian River County students can benefit from these scholarship opportunities as they prepare for college.

cards.headline: Florida Supreme Court Adopts New AI Rules for Courtrooms Effective June 15
cards.teaser: Florida attorneys and self-represented litigants will be required to certify that what they cite in court exists and is accurate under new rules adopted by the Florida Supreme Court.
cards.body:
The Florida Supreme Court recently adopted new rules addressing the misuse of artificial intelligence in courtrooms, with the rules taking effect June 15. Florida attorneys and self-represented litigants will be required to certify that what they cite in court exists and is accurate. Sanctions for violations could range from a public reprimand to fines and even suspension. Federal Judge William Matthewman, chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, has been involved in efforts to control how AI is used in courts after its misuse became rampant in his own courtroom. Matthewman said he sees the situation getting worse before it gets better, noting that while the Florida Supreme Court's order will help in Florida, he has seen the problem growing over the last couple of years.

In Polk County, an attorney representing the Polk County School District in an ongoing lawsuit over school bus cameras was recently chastised after a judge discovered fabricated facts and cited cases that don't exist were filed as part of a motion to dismiss the case. In his apology to the court, the attorney said he used ChatGPT as a drafting and research aid but admitted there was no excuse for his failure to verify before filing. A spokesperson for the school district said it takes accuracy and integrity in legal proceedings seriously and is reviewing the matter to determine if the attorney will be eligible for contracted services again in the future.

cards.headline: Florida Could Ban Fireworks for Fourth of July Due to Severe Drought
cards.teaser: Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson warned the state could ban fireworks for the Fourth of July's 250th anniversary celebration as drought conditions worsen across the state, including Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
State leaders are weighing whether to ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence as drought conditions intensify across Florida. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was put in place. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with areas including Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about the possibility of a ban, stating that if drought conditions persist through the Fourth of July, a ban is likely. Simpson noted the potential danger of hundreds of thousands of people using fireworks simultaneously statewide. The Department of Agriculture indicated a fireworks ban would be a last resort. hero.body:
Mary Hubbard of Okeechobee County has filed a lawsuit against Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart, claiming she discovered live worms in a can of SpaghettiOs purchased from the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. The alleged contamination occurred in June 2024. According to the complaint, Hubbard and her daughter both became ill after consuming the product, developing parasitic infections and other medical complications as a result of the incident.

Hubbard's legal team states that she observed what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving inside the food. To document the discovery, Hubbard recorded multiple videos showing worm-like organisms moving throughout the SpaghettiOs. These videos are being presented as evidence in the case. The lawsuit contends that Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart failed to properly inspect the product before it reached consumers, allowing the contaminated food to be sold to the public.

The complaint seeks 50,000 dollars in damages for the alleged harm caused to Hubbard and her daughter. Campbell Soup Co. has responded by stating that the claims lack merit and do not have a valid basis. Walmart indicated that the company is currently reviewing the court filing and has not yet provided a substantive response to the allegations.

This case highlights concerns about food safety and quality control in mass-produced food products sold at major retailers. The lawsuit represents an effort to hold both the manufacturer and the retailer accountable for what the plaintiff alleges was a failure in their inspection and safety protocols. As the case proceeds through the court system, it may shed light on the procedures these companies use to identify and prevent contaminated products from reaching store shelves.

cards.headline: Clearwater Threshers defeat St. Lucie Mets 10-4 in Friday game
cards.teaser: The Clearwater Threshers cruised to a 10-4 victory over the St. Lucie Mets on Friday.
cards.body:
The Clearwater Threshers defeated the St. Lucie Mets 10-4 in a game played Friday. The win came after the teams had previously met in a doubleheader on Wednesday, when the Threshers swept both games.

The Tuesday game between the two teams had been postponed. The Threshers put together a strong offensive performance in Friday's contest to secure the victory over the Mets.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway to make way for mixed-use development
cards.teaser: Crews began demolition this week on portions of the Indian River Mall in Vero Beach, starting the first phase of a major redevelopment project for the shopping .
cards.body:
Crews began demolition this week on portions of the Indian River Mall in Vero Beach as part of a revitalization project for the shopping center. Project manager Joseph Scarfone said the first phase involves taking down the Macy's building and the former Sears location. The site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with approximately 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants, and possible residential spaces.

Neighbors watching the demolition from the mall parking lot expressed their views on the project. Vero Beach resident Mary Alice Stopyra said the mall had degraded over time and expressed happiness about the demolition. Mark Manera, who has visited the mall for years, described it as looking like "the death of a beautiful building" and said he witnessed a steady decline year after year over 12 years. However, Manera said change is needed and that bringing new life, jobs, and opportunities would be wonderful. Scarfone said the redevelopment will transform the site rather than leaving "a dead mall for the last 12 years that was getting cobwebs," calling it "a city within a city." He hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027, with the development team still working on permitting for the remaining phases.

cards.headline: Martin and St. Lucie counties face millions in losses from property tax referendum
cards.teaser: A Florida Association of Counties study estimates Martin County could lose $50 million in 2027-28 and St. Lucie County could lose $80 million under a new property tax reform referendum.
cards.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of a new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. A study from the Florida Association of Counties estimates the financial losses counties could face: Martin County could lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29, while St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County faces estimated losses of $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29, and Okeechobee County could lose $4 million in 2027-28 and $7 million in 2028-29. Palm Beach County could lose $280 million in 2027-28 and $523 million in 2028-29.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are possibilities if the referendum passes. Powell noted that officials do not yet know if revenue would come from an increase in sales tax or user fees for other services. Powell is restricted by state law from speaking out against or endorsing the referendum but can offer educational information about it. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal provides relief for families in $300,000 homes working multiple jobs. Voters will decide the referendum in November.

cards.headline: Glades Day Gators football targets state championship after 4-9 season
cards.teaser: The Glades Day Gators in Belle Glade are putting in summer work with hopes of winning their first state title since 2010.
cards.body:
The Glades Day Gators are putting in the work this summer, sweating through the heat and humidity in Belle Glade with one goal in mind: a return to state championship glory. The Gators finished last season with a 4-9 record but made a run in the SSAA playoffs, reaching the third round before their season ended. Head coach James Threlkeld said the playoff push offered a valuable lesson. "The way we were able to turn it around in the playoffs, that was a lesson learned," Threlkeld said. "I think, more for our kids, that was just kind of a decision they made, so we're trying to carry over that mindset."

Threlkeld emphasized that the summer months are critical for building toward a strong fall campaign. "Getting yourself acclimated to the heat and the humidity is only gonna help us whenever we start camping," he said. "You know they have helmets and pads on, and I think that's a key part." The Gators last won a state title in 2010. Senior Ramsey Rimes said adding another championship would be meaningful: "It would be a great senior year if we finish it off. Hopefully, we got it this year." Fellow senior Preston Sanford echoed that sentiment, saying "To break that streak, that would mean a lot."

hero.headline: Weekend activities planned across Treasure Coast
hero.teaser: Multiple events are scheduled for the weekend across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.
hero.body:
The Treasure Coast has activities scheduled for the weekend of June 6-7. Events are taking place in communities throughout the region.

Families and residents have options for entertainment and recreation this Saturday and Sunday. The weekend programming includes various venues and activities across the three-county area.

Events are happening in multiple Treasure Coast cities. Residents can find activities throughout Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties during the weekend.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Air Show security operation underway
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Air Show is relying on a coordinated security operation involving multiple agencies and personnel.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Air Show requires a massive security operation coordinated by multiple agencies. The event draws large crowds and features military aircraft demonstrations requiring extensive safety protocols.

Security planning for the air show involves coordination between local law enforcement, military personnel, and emergency services. The operation ensures public safety during the aviation performances and manages crowd control throughout the venue.

The air show takes place in Vero Beach with security teams positioned throughout the event grounds and surrounding areas. Officials have implemented protocols to handle the influx of visitors and protect both spectators and performers during the demonstrations.

cards.headline: Stars and Stripes Park opens in Port St. Lucie with veteran tributes
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie has opened Stars and Stripes Park, a new facility honoring military veterans. The park includes tributes recognizing those who served in the armed forces.

The opening took place Thursday in Port St. Lucie. The park was designed to provide a dedicated space for veteran recognition and community gatherings.

Stars and Stripes Park features memorial elements celebrating military service. The facility adds to Port St. Lucie's network of public parks and recreational spaces.

The park is now open to the public. Residents can visit the site to view the veteran tributes and use the park facilities.

hero.headline: Florida considers statewide fireworks ban for Fourth of July's 250th anniversary due to severe drought
hero.body:
Florida state leaders are examining whether to implement a statewide ban on fireworks for this year's Fourth of July celebration as drought conditions have reached levels not seen since 1998, when the state last prohibited fireworks across the entire state. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services has determined that current drought conditions are even more severe than those that prompted the 1998 ban. Every part of Florida is experiencing at least abnormally dry conditions, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast facing moderate to extreme drought situations.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson warned about the potential ban earlier in the year, recognizing both the importance of celebrating the nation's 250th anniversary and the serious fire risks posed by widespread fireworks use. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said in May. He emphasized that officials should explore alternative celebration methods, saying "We all love the 250th celebration we're gonna have this year, but we probably ought to be considering alternatives."

Despite the drought concerns, Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach has experienced increased customer activity as people prepare for the holiday. Bill Murphy, who works at the store, said the business closely monitors drought conditions to determine whether it is safe for fireworks use. Murphy expressed cautious optimism about the situation, pointing to weather forecasts that predict significant rainfall. "We always keep a close eye on the drought index to make sure the ground is saturated enough, but the reality is there's plenty of rain in the forecast," Murphy said.

The Department of Agriculture has indicated that a statewide fireworks ban would be a last resort measure, though the severity of current drought conditions has prompted serious deliberation about whether such action will become necessary. State officials continue to monitor conditions as the Fourth of July approaches to determine whether celebrating the nation's 250th anniversary will require residents to find alternatives to traditional fireworks displays.

cards.headline: Florida dive operators fight federal shark feeding ban, warn of tourism and conservation impacts
cards.teaser: A federal bill to ban shark feeding in waters within 200 miles of Florida has cleared the U.S. House, drawing sharp criticism from dive operators who say it unfairly targets their conservation-driven businesses.
cards.body:
The Safe Florida Seas Act, H.R. 3831, would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters call it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, a coalition of dive operators contends the bill unfairly targets their work, often veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education, conservation and responsible shark encounters, while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said no one from Congress has asked operators to present data or explain their practices. Operators say they avoid surface chumming by taking bait underwater during dives, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food, unlike some commercial harvesting operations that release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface.

The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent. However, Florida operators and some researchers say the Hawaii experience tells a different story. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents have increased, fatalities have been reported and, according to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch. Campbell has sent a letter to Congress urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings suspends gubernatorial campaign after prostate cancer diagnosis
cards.teaser: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings announced he has been diagnosed with prostate cancer and is suspending his gubernatorial campaign, drawing messages of support from Republicans and Democrats across Florida.
cards.body:
Political allies and rivals across party lines are expressing support for Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings following his prostate cancer diagnosis and decision to suspend his gubernatorial campaign. Republican gubernatorial front-runner Byron Donalds wrote on X that he hopes "the Lord watch over the Demings family, provide them with strength and comfort, and bless Jerry with a swift recovery." Former U.S. Representative David Jolly, who faced Demings in the Democratic primary, said Demings has dedicated his life to public service and will bring that same spirit to this new chapter.

U.S. Rep. Maxwell Frost, an Orlando Democrat, wrote that Demings has always been a fighter for Orange County and will face this challenge with the same strength. Democrat state Sen. Shevrin Jones said Demings has spent a lifetime showing up for others and now it's their turn to support him. Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava called Demings a man of extraordinary strength demonstrated throughout his decades in law enforcement and public office. Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback said he and his wife will keep Demings in their prayers throughout treatment. Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said Demings has served with commitment and compassion for decades. Florida GOP Chair Evan Power also asked for prayers for Demings and his family. Governor Ron DeSantis, whose administration once threatened to remove Demings to pressure him into signing an immigration agreement, did not immediately post a statement on social media about the diagnosis.

cards.headline: Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody files legislation to strengthen penalties for harming police animals
cards.teaser: The Plant City Republican filed the LEO K-9 Protection Act, which strengthens penalties for anyone who intentionally harms animals, including canine officers and patrol horses.
cards.body:
Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody, a Plant City Republican, filed the LEO K-9 Protection Act to strengthen penalties for anyone who intentionally harms police animals, including canine officers and patrol horses. Moody said highly trained animals help law enforcement apprehend dangerous criminals, detect narcotics and explosives, assist with searches, find missing persons and save lives. She emphasized that law enforcement animals serving with brave men and women protect communities and deserve protection in return.

The legislation is named for K-9 Leo, a Marion County canine deputy who was shot and killed in the line of duty in 2024. In addition to increasing penalties for using deadly weapons against law enforcement animals, the bill directs the U.S. Department of Transportation to issue regulations permitting emergency medical service providers to transport injured police animals at their discretion. The measure mirrors legislation already introduced in the House by Rep. Aaron Bean, a Fernandina Beach Republican. Moody wants violence against police animals treated as an aggravating factor in criminal cases, similar to how assaulting a law enforcement officer is currently handled.

cards.headline: Secretary of State Marco Rubio faces questions from Florida lawmakers on Cuba, Venezuela, and vaccine policy
cards.teaser: The former Florida Senator returned to Capitol Hill for meetings with members of the state's congressional delegation, answering questions about foreign policy in the Americas and international vaccine distribution.
cards.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio returned to Capitol Hill for meetings with Florida's congressional delegation, where he fielded questions on Cuba, Venezuela, and vaccine policy. Rick Scott, a Naples Republican, praised the recent indictment of former Cuban President Raúl Castro and the arrest of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, saying Castro's indictment sparked renewed hope for a free Cuba with government accountability and political freedom. Rubio noted that Vice President Delcy Rodriguez is serving as acting President of Venezuela under U.S. authority and stated that Venezuela is in a better place than five months ago, though it ultimately needs multiparty, free and fair elections. Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Coral Gables Republican, stressed there can be no democratic future for Cuba that leaves the Castro family in power and no lasting stability in Venezuela without free and fair elections.

Rep. Lois Frankel, a West Palm Beach Democrat, questioned Rubio about administration pressure on the Gavi Alliance to limit international vaccine availability, citing disagreements with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy. Rubio disagreed with the characterization of Kennedy and clarified that the State Department, not the HHS Secretary, would oversee the Gavi Alliance moving forward. Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart, a Hialeah Republican, urged Rubio to consider measures to limit China's influence in the Western Hemisphere. Rubio said American contractors need to be available to provide infrastructure services as readily as Chinese competitors.

cards.headline: State Senator Nick DiCeglie endorses Kathleen Peters for Pinellas County Commission re-election
cards.teaser: DiCeglie described Peters as a civil servant with unwavering dedication to communities and called her the conservative choice for the Pinellas County Commission.
cards.body:
State Senator Nick DiCeglie endorsed Pinellas County Commissioner Kathleen Peters in her re-election bid for the District 6 seat, calling her a civil servant with "unwavering dedication to our communities" and the "conservative choice for the Pinellas County Commission." DiCeglie noted that Peters has "consistently demonstrated fiscal responsibility while leading on critical local issues like storm resiliency and beach renourishment." Peters said she was honored to earn DiCeglie's support and shares his commitment to protecting taxpayers, making Pinellas affordable again, and ensuring neighborhoods are safe places to live and raise a family. The endorsement comes about a week after Peters secured support from U.S. Representative Anna Paulina Luna and follows a recent endorsement from Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri.

Peters, a Republican, is seeking her second re-election to the dais after first securing a spot in 2018. She faces Democratic challenger David Glenn Jr. As of the end of March, Peters has raised $126,000 via her official campaign account and $24,500 through her affiliated political committee, Florida Speaks, while Glenn has raised $3,400. Peters benefits from a significant voter registration advantage in District 6, where there are 23,000 more Republicans than Democrats, a 25-percentage-point advantage. Peters previously served in the Florida House from 2012 to 2018 and as Mayor of South Pasadena before that. She now serves on a Commission with a GOP supermajority, with just one Democrat sharing the dais.

The threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breakthrough would transform a narrow land strip into an open inlet. This scenario has historical precedent. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers restored it with sand fill. Mark Perry from the Florida Oceanographic Society warns that another breach would destabilize ecosystems requiring a precise balance between fresh and saltwater to function. He also notes the consequences reach far beyond the shoreline itself.

The stakes include significant natural and cultural resources. The Joseph Reed Mound, an archaeological site dating back 3,000 to 4,000 years, has already lost half its mass to erosion. Wildlife refuges at risk include Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry points out that over 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. A separate state assessment indicates erosion threatens mangrove swamps essential for habitat and coastal defense, while elevated water levels could displace entire species across the island. Perry emphasizes that sea levels have risen since the 1950s and have accelerated over the last 15 years, requiring collaborative approaches to address the problem.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field confirmed the town battles erosion through continuous maintenance efforts. In April 2025, the community completed a substantial beach renourishment initiative, adding sand equivalent to filling nearly 400 Olympic-sized pools. While oceanfront homes face no immediate danger, Field stressed this security depends entirely on ongoing maintenance work. He characterized the current approach as repeatedly applying a temporary solution. About $3 million in local taxpayer funding supports beach renourishment annually. Field cautioned that a potential breach would demand significant state and federal investment for repairs. He indicated the recent FDEP assessment strengthens Jupiter Island's position to secure state and federal funding for erosion mitigation efforts.

Field emphasized that sustained funding remains uncertain. He warned that discontinuing beach renourishment support would trigger rapid and widespread coastal changes across Florida that residents would likely regret. The island's future depends on maintaining this investment in protective measures.

hero.headline: Summer fertilizer ban takes effect June 1 in St. Lucie, Martin, and Indian River counties
hero.teaser: Residents can no longer use fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on lawns or landscaping through September 30.
hero.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties must stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. This restriction remains in place until September 30. The ban aims to address environmental concerns during Florida's wet season, when heavy rainfall can carry nutrient-laden runoff into local waterways.

According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the fertilizer ban is designed to reduce nutrient-rich runoff that contributes to algae blooms during the rainy season. These blooms pose a significant threat to important water systems including the Indian River Lagoon and the St. Lucie River. Skaggs explained that algae can prevent sunlight from reaching beneficial aquatic plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. Beyond ecological damage, certain algae blooms become dangerous at high concentrations, releasing toxins that threaten human health and damage entire ecosystems.

For residents looking for alternatives during the ban period, Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective solution for gardens and landscaping. Ricketts noted that composting can be accomplished simply and affordably using everyday materials. He suggested that a small trash can provides an easy and practical method for creating compost and adding necessary nutrients to lawns and landscaped areas without relying on chemical fertilizers.

The ban reflects growing concerns about water quality in the region. As Florida experiences its summer storm season, the combination of heavy rainfall and nutrient runoff from residential and commercial properties can overwhelm local waterways. By temporarily restricting fertilizer use during these critical months, the three counties hope to protect their aquatic environments and the communities that depend on them. Residents should plan ahead during the summer months and consider composting as a sustainable alternative to maintain their landscapes while supporting regional environmental protection efforts.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie burglary suspect arrested after homeowner watches break-in on security camera
cards.teaser: Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, was arrested and charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling after a Port St.
cards.body:
Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, was arrested and charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling after a Port St. Lucie resident caught him breaking into an apartment on his home security camera Thursday afternoon. The incident occurred at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in the 5400 block of NW Moorehen Trail around 3:38 p.m. The apartment resident received a motion alert from his security system while away from home and checked his live camera feed, where he spotted a masked man inside his apartment. The resident activated his camera's audible siren, causing the suspect to leave briefly, but the man returned and tampered with the camera itself.

Multiple witnesses saw the suspect flee the victim's apartment and enter a neighboring unit in the same building. When Port St. Lucie Police arrived, they found clear signs of forced entry, including damage to the front door and door frame. Officers established a perimeter while the SWAT team was called to assist. After repeated announcements, Thibodeau exited the apartment and surrendered without incident. Investigators collected surveillance footage from multiple sources throughout the complex, including doorbell cameras that captured a man matching the suspect's description before and after the burglary. Police found evidence that Thibodeau attempted to obstruct security cameras and that a watch valued at approximately $300 was stolen. Thibodeau was transported to the St. Lucie County jail.

cards.headline: Erosion threatens to split Jupiter Island, endangering St. Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park
cards.teaser: A new state report warns that erosion at Peck Lake could breach the island and disrupt ecosystems affecting St. Lucie County conservation lands.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake and endangers wildlife refuges including Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge and St. Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. The report also identified the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, as at risk. According to the report, over 33 threatened and endangered species live in these areas.

Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems dependent on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater. A second state assessment warned erosion is threatening mangrove swamps critical for habitat and coastal protection. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town fights erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a beach renourishment project that dumped enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment annually, and if funding for beach renourishment in Florida ends, the state's coastline will change quickly.

hero.headline: Fertilizer Ban Takes Effect June 30 in Indian River County
hero.body:
Starting June 30, residents of Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties must stop applying fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen to their lawns and landscaping. The restriction marks an effort to address environmental concerns during Florida's rainy season.

Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that the ban targets nutrient-rich runoff that flows into local waterways during heavy rainfall. This runoff can trigger algae blooms in sensitive ecosystems like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. The excessive growth of algae disrupts the natural balance of these waterways and their wildlife populations. "It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," Skaggs said. In some cases, the algae blooms become particularly dangerous. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health."

For residents looking to maintain their landscapes during the ban period, composting offers a practical alternative. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective way to provide nutrients to gardens and landscaping without relying on commercial fertilizers. According to Ricketts, "It can be like a small trash can. That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." This approach allows homeowners to recycle organic waste while naturally enriching their soil.

The ban applies across three counties and represents a regional commitment to protecting Florida's waterways from the effects of nutrient pollution. Residents should plan ahead before the June 30 deadline to transition their lawn care practices and explore composting solutions for their gardening needs.
